results.name: trial_index_slope
results.description: OLS slope of yes (rating) on trial_index/100 across all trials; observed more negative than null means people grow more conservative over the session while the model (no trial dependence) predicts a flat rate.

results.name: cell_unanimity
results.description: Fraction of (number_set, target) cells with >=2 responses where all responses agree; observed above null means people are more consistent/extreme than the model's graded p_yes (model probabilities too intermediate), below means people are noisier.

results.name: example_as_target_yes
results.description: Yes rate on trials whose target is itself one of the shown examples; observed below null means the model over-predicts certain yes for already-seen examples (people do not treat examples as guaranteed members).

results.name: parity_match_effect
results.description: For multi-example sets whose examples all share parity, yes rate for targets of the same parity minus targets of the opposite parity (targets in set excluded); observed above null means people use parity more than the model, below means the model over-produces parity-based generalization.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_effect
# description: For multi-example sets whose examples all share parity, yes rate for targets of the same parity minus targets of the opposite parity (targets in set excluded); observed above null means people use parity more than the model, below means the model over-produces parity-based generalization.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    n = (s.str.count(",") + 1).to_numpy()
    ex = s.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    par = np.mod(np.where(valid, ex, 0), 2)
    n_odd = (par * valid).sum(axis=1)
    all_even = (n_odd == 0)
    all_odd = (n_odd == n)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    in_set = (ex == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & (all_even | all_odd) & ~in_set
    set_par = np.where(all_odd, 1, 0)
    same = base & ((t % 2) == set_par)
    diff = base & ((t % 2) != set_par)
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    if same.sum() == 0 or diff.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[same].mean() - y[diff].mean())

results.name: single_example_yes
results.description: Yes rate on single-example sets with target different from the example (breadth of generalization from one number); observed above null means people generalize more broadly from one example than the model, below means less.

results.name: decade_vs_units_digit_share
results.description: Among targets (not in the set) that share at least one digit with some example, yes rate when the target's tens digit equals some example's tens digit (same decade) minus yes rate when the shared digit(s) do not include a decade match; observed above null means people weight positional tens-digit/decade matches more than the model's position-free contains-digit concepts, below means less.
results.code:
# name: decade_vs_units_digit_share
# description: Among targets (not in the set) that share at least one digit with some example, yes rate when the target's tens digit equals some example's tens digit (same decade) minus yes rate when the shared digit(s) do not include a decade match; observed above null means people weight positional tens-digit/decade matches more than the model's position-free contains-digit concepts, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    exi = np.where(valid, ex, -1000).astype(int)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    t2 = t[:, None]
    in_set = (exi == t2).any(axis=1)
    def digits(a):
        a = np.asarray(a)
        tens = np.where(a >= 10, (a // 10) % 10, -1)
        units = a % 10
        hund = np.where(a >= 100, 1, -1)
        return tens, units, hund
    et, eu, eh = digits(exi)
    tt, tu, th = digits(t2)
    tt0 = np.where(t2 >= 100, 0, tt)  # 100 has tens digit 0
    et0 = np.where(exi >= 100, 0, et)
    share = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool)
    for a in (et0, eu, eh):
        for b in (tt0, tu, th):
            share |= (valid & (a == b) & (a >= 0)).any(axis=1)
    decade = (valid & (et0 == tt0) & (tt0 >= 0)).any(axis=1)
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    base = share & ~in_set
    A = base & decade
    B = base & ~decade
    if A.sum() == 0 or B.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[A].mean() - y[B].mean())

results.name: n_examples_slope_multi
results.description: OLS slope of yes on number of examples (2-4 example sets only, targets not in the set); observed above null means people's generalization narrows less (or widens) with more examples than the model's size principle predicts, below means it narrows more.
results.code:
# name: n_examples_slope_multi
# description: OLS slope of yes on number of examples (2-4 example sets only, targets not in the set); observed above null means people's generalization narrows less (or widens) with more examples than the model's size principle predicts, below means it narrows more.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    n = (s.str.count(",") + 1).to_numpy().astype(float)
    ex = s.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()[:, None]
    in_set = (ex == t).any(axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & ~in_set
    x = n[m]
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)[m]
    if len(x) < 2:
        return 0.0
    xc = x - x.mean()
    denom = (xc ** 2).sum()
    if denom == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float((xc * (y - y.mean())).sum() / denom)

results.name: distance_gradient
results.description: Yes rate for targets within 3 of the nearest example minus yes rate for targets >=15 from the nearest example (targets equal to an example excluded); observed below null means the model over-produces a numerical-similarity (interval) gradient that people don't show, above means people rely more on magnitude proximity.
results.code:
# name: distance_gradient
# description: Yes rate for targets within 3 of the nearest example minus yes rate for targets >=15 from the nearest example (targets equal to an example excluded); observed below null means the model over-produces a numerical-similarity (interval) gradient that people don't show, above means people rely more on magnitude proximity.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()[:, None]
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t), axis=1)
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    near = (d >= 1) & (d <= 3)
    far = d >= 15
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[near].mean() - y[far].mean())
